name: filterer
intent: Make filtering a first-class value: a container-like object hands out a filterer - a small object whose one operation takes a caller-supplied criterion and returns a filtered copy of the container's own type - so criteria are supplied by callers, named, composed and tested outside the container instead of being hard-coded as one method per criterion.
problem: Filtering logic is hard-wired into the container that owns the elements: every criterion becomes another method (findExpired, findExpiredNotNotified, findByGenreAndAuthor), every combination another method, callers cannot pass a criterion they already hold, and the criteria cannot be tested, logged or reused outside the container. In languages with use-site variance the same design collapses at the first subtyped container: an inherited filtered(Predicate<? super Item>) cannot be overridden to accept a Predicate<? super ScoredItem>, so subtypes accumulate ad-hoc narrowing methods (scoreFiltered, scoreExplanatoryFiltered) that are pure boilerplate.
context: Containers that own a collection of elements and must hand out selections of them - aggregate-like domain objects (a group of items, a threat-aware system, a catalogue), repository finders, view models and pipeline stages - where criteria vary, combine or come from the caller, where the result must stay the container's own type (identity, unit, labels and invariants preserved), and where the language offers first-class functions, function objects or languages' predicate types to carry the criterion.
benefits: Criteria become values: a predicate can be built, named, stored, passed across layers, logged and reused, instead of being reachable only through a method of the container.
The container stays closed for modification: new criteria arrive from the caller, so no new findByX/findByY method (and no method per combination) is needed for every rule.

Subtype-friendly in variance-limited languages: the filterer is requested covariantly, so a subtyped container narrows the element type once instead of adding one narrowed filtering method per inheritance level.
Criteria compose: and/or/not over predicates yields new criteria without touching the container or the elements.
Testability: each criterion is a small pure function over one element and is exercised without a container, database or fixture.
Selection is separated from storage and domain logic: the container owns its elements and its identity, the caller owns the question being asked.
One documented filtering entry point covers every current and future criterion, which keeps the container's API surface small and uniform.
tradeoffs: Indirection before reuse: for a criterion used at one call site a plain condition or lambda is shorter; the filterer type and its generic parameters only pay for themselves once criteria are passed around, composed, named or tested separately.

The filtered result is a copy: an eager filterer allocates a second container per call and per step in a chain, and the cost hides behind a fluent call site; lazy forms avoid the copy but re-evaluate the criteria on every traversal.

Non-idempotent criteria break the contract: predicates with counters, lazy loads or side effects give different results on the second traversal (re-enumerated LINQ queries, re-traversed views, consumed iterators) and the failure is silent.

In languages with first-class functions but no use-site variance the filterer type is largely ceremony: a plain function parameter already carries the criterion, so the extra interface is a design tax paid for symmetry with the classic form.
Diagnostics get harder: after filtered(keep) returns a smaller container nothing records why an element was rejected, so callers who must explain a rejection end up re-implementing the predicate.
Error handling across the boundary: a predicate that throws or loads data mid-traversal fails halfway, leaving a partially filtered result or a broken iterator instead of a clean failure.
A filter is not an authorisation or validation boundary: a criterion that fails open (a null owner, an unrecognised role) silently widens the selection instead of denying it.

Sharing storage shortcuts the contract: when the filtered copy aliases the source's backing array - common with filter-in-place or retained slices - later writes to the source appear inside the 'filtered' container.

participants.responsibility: Owns the elements and their identity/metadata and exposes the single filtering entry point (filtered(), filtered(keep), filter(predicate)) that returns a filterer bound to this container.
The contained type the criteria are stated over; the container's element type (or a supertype of it) is the domain of every predicate it accepts.

The first-class filter: a function object or function value that takes one criterion and returns a filtered copy of the container's own type; in most languages it is the container's method reference rather than a written class.
The caller-supplied condition over an element - lambda, closure, function pointer with context, function object or type-guarded predicate - optionally composed from smaller criteria.
Chooses, composes and passes criteria and decides whether a materialised filtered copy or a lazy view of it is wanted.
Narrows the element type and re-declares the filterer covariantly so callers can filter by members of the subtype without new narrowing methods.

use_cases: Threat/telemetry dashboards: a system object holding detected threats returns a filtered copy of itself by threat type or by probability, keeping the system id and metadata, so a new detection criterion needs no new method on the system.
Catalogue and library search: availability, author, genre and publication-year criteria are combined at runtime into one predicate instead of one method per combination.

Repository and collection APIs where the criterion comes from the caller: the repository exposes one generic filtered(keep) instead of dozens of findBy... methods, and callers keep their own named criteria.
Stream and batch processing: each stage is an independently testable criterion value chained over records — the shape stream-processing pipelines and log filters rely on.
View models and UI facets: a presentation object filters its own rows by the facets the user selected and returns a same-typed view object with the same identity.
Test and simulation fixtures: the production criteria are reused to select scenario data, so tests exercise the same predicate the application runs.

Access-scoped views over owned data: a container hands out a filtered copy limited to the visible subset (an audit or per-tenant view) — provided the criterion is a convenience layer over real enforcement, never the enforcement itself.

CQRS read models and projection views: a read model aggregates events into a state container; filtering by event type, aggregate ID or time window returns a same-typed view for queries without modifying the write model.

Multi-tenant SaaS data isolation: a tenant-scoped container returns a filtered view of its own data, preserving the tenant ID and metadata as identity while restricting the element set to the tenant's subset.
Event-sourcing subscribers: a subscriber holds a queue of events and returns a filtered sub-queue filtered by event type or stream ID, keeping the subscriber's offset and identity.
Audit and compliance reporting: a log aggregate returns a filtered copy by date range, severity or actor, preserving the aggregate's metadata (source, stream ID) in each result row.

Reactive streams and publish-subscribe: a stream source implements filtered() returning a new publisher that emits only the elements satisfying the subscriber's predicate, decoupling producer and consumer filtering logic.

ETL and data-pipeline staging: each pipeline stage wraps an upstream container, filters it by a stage-specific predicate, and passes the result downstream — stages are independently testable criterion objects.
Domain-driven design aggregates: an aggregate root exposes a filtered view of its entity collection for reporting queries, keeping the aggregate's invariants and identity intact.

Rails index filtering (dobtco/filterer gem): a PersonFilterer class turns each request parameter into a param_... method over the relation so controllers call Person.filter(params) instead of accumulating where-clauses - the pattern's name adopted by a real library, though the result there is a built query rather than a same-typed container copy.

.NET query-DTO filtering (enisn/AutoFilterer): ApplyFilter compiles a filter DTO into a LINQ expression tree applied to the queryable, so the caller holds a first-class, inspectable criterion (OpenAPI 3.0-compatible) instead of a per-entity findBy... method.

Composable stream criteria (redru/filters): a Filter<T> assembled with filtering()/thenFiltering()/objectEquals is a named, reusable criterion value passed to stream().filter(filter) - the criteria-as-values half of the pattern without a container wrapper.
avoid_when: The condition is used at exactly one call site and never combined, named or tested: write it inline or pass a plain lambda - the extra filterer type adds nothing.

The language and its collections already give you criteria as first-class values and the container type carries no identity or invariants: use the native filter (list.filter(pred), Where, streams) and skip the wrapper.
The criteria are authored or edited by business users at runtime: that is a rule engine or expression DSL, not a filterer compiled into the code.
The criteria are really store mechanics (index hints, joins, pagination, SQL fragments): use a query object or the repository's query API and keep translation out of the container.
The goal is to remove elements in place from a container you own and the language supports it (retain, removeIf, DeleteFunc): filtering into a fresh copy on every call is wasted allocation.
The result must be a different type or a projection (rows, ids, DTOs): that is a mapping or query-object decision; a filterer preserves the container's own type by design.
anti_patterns: Criteria hidden in the filterer: the container reads configuration, a clock or a global to decide what 'filtered' means, so the same call returns different sets in test and production.
Aliasing instead of copying: filtered() returns a wrapper or a slice over the original storage, so later mutations of the source leak into the filtered result.
Eager chain churn: filtered(a).filtered(b).filtered(c) materialises a new container per step where one composed predicate would be a single pass.

Stateful predicates: counters, caches or logging inside the criterion make the result depend on traversal order and on the number of traversals — the bug behind 'the filtered list is wrong the second time'.
Filter-as-security: using a criterion as the access check for data (failing open on a null owner) turns a selection convenience into a data leak.
Stringly-typed criteria: a filterer parameterised by field names and operators ('status', 'eq', 'closed') rebuilds an accidental rules engine and loses compile-time checking.
One subclass per criterion: Filter classes that exist only to hold a boolean expression, adding types, files and tests without adding meaning.
Predicate explosion: combinatorial explosion of optional filters (2^n possibilities) without composing at the predicate level forces new method overloads for each combination.
Boxing in primitive streams: using Predicate<Object> on IntStream/LongStream elements forces boxing per element, defeating the purpose of primitive streams in high-throughput pipelines.

Null criterion silently widening: treating a null predicate as 'no filter' without an explicit check widens the selection in ways callers may not anticipate, especially when the null comes from a missing query parameter.
design_principles: Open/closed principle: new criteria do not modify the container - closed for modification, open for extension.
Separation of concerns: owning elements, stating a criterion and deciding what to do with the selection are three different jobs.
Composition over inheritance: criteria compose as values (and/or/not) instead of deepening a hierarchy of filter subclasses.
Dependency inversion and least knowledge: the container depends on the predicate abstraction and exposes one entry point, not on the concrete criteria callers will use.
Variance discipline: accept the widest criterion the container can honour (a predicate over a supertype of its element) and return the container's own most specific type.
Information hiding: how elements are stored, copied or lazily traversed stays inside the container.
best_practices: Keep the filterer pure: it evaluates the criterion and returns a new container, with no logging, mutation or I/O inside, so the same call can be repeated with the same answer. Stateful predicates (lazy loads, clock reads, counters) silently break the second traversal.

Return a copy of the container's own type with identity and metadata preserved (id, unit, labels, invariants). A bare element list loses the meaning callers depend on; a live view of internal storage leaks source mutations into the 'filtered' result.

Accept a contravariant criterion type — a predicate over a supertype of the element (Predicate<? super E>) — so callers can pass broad criteria without casting, and declare the return covariantly (Filterer<? extends G, ? extends E>) so subtypes narrow without new methods.
Name reusable criteria after the domain question (OverdueInvoice, RootkitsOnly, HasActiveSubscription) and keep them as named values or constants, not inline lambdas repeated at call sites.

Choose the evaluation model deliberately and document it: materialise when the container type is required (always returns a new container); use lazy forms (iterators, streams, views) for chained pipelines and document that re-traversal re-evaluates predicates.
Compose criteria with combinators (predicate.and().or().negate(), boolean operators in one lambda) instead of chaining separate filtered() calls, which allocates a new container per step.

Never let the filterer be the only explanation of a rejection. Instrument at the call site, return the failing predicate alongside the result, or use a result type that carries the reason — downstream code that must explain exclusions cannot reconstruct the predicate's logic.
Type the criterion parameter to reject unrelated types at compile time, not validate them at runtime. Prefer Predicate<? super E> over raw Predicate or Object.

Avoid boxing overhead in hot paths when filtering primitive streams: IntPredicate, LongPredicate, DoublePredicate avoid boxing per element; for domain objects prefer a dedicated functional interface over the generic Predicate<Object>.

Handle null elements explicitly: a null that passes the predicate crashes the stream; a null criterion itself should be treated as 'no filter' (return all) or rejected with a clear error — never silently ignored.

Test the predicate in isolation from the container: a criterion is a pure function of one element and requires no fixture, database, or mock to verify; this is the filterer's main testability advantage.

Keep filtering and authorisation on different layers: a filterer is a convenience layer, never the enforcement mechanism. When a criterion fails it should widen the result, not deny access — failing open is a security bug, not a filtering convenience.

Consider the impact of concurrent modification when the source collection is modified between lazy re-evaluations: use a snapshot (defensive copy) at the point of filtering when the source may be concurrently written.

When composing many optional criteria (e.g., 10 UI filters where only 3 are active), return a conjunction of always-true predicates for absent filters so the composed predicate is always safe to evaluate without null guards.

In languages with pattern matching or expression-tree support (C#, Java JPA Criteria), prefer inspectable criteria objects over opaque lambdas when the criteria must be translated to queries, serialised, or logged as data.
sources: Tomasz Linkowski, Filterer Pattern (2018) — the pattern's origin: a container-like object returns filtered versions of itself through a Filterer<G, E> functional interface (G by(Predicate<? super E>)), first published on DZone on 4 June 2018 and expanded in a 10-step tutorial on 31 January 2019.
https://blog.tlinkowski.pl/2018/filterer-pattern/ — canonical article by the pattern author, covering the core interface, generic form, syntactic-sugar default methods, and subtype covariance.

https://blog.tlinkowski.pl/2019/filterer-pattern-in-10-steps/ — extended 10-step tutorial demonstrating the pattern's emergence through progressive requirements, including subtype covariance, parametric form, and detection of the right moment to introduce it.

https://github.com/tlinkowski/filterer-pattern-in-10-steps — reference implementation (Apache 2.0) with three model variants (subtyping, parametric-composition, parametric-subtype) for each of the 10 steps.

https://java-design-patterns.com/patterns/filterer/ — community-maintained Java Design Patterns site entry, covering the pattern's motivation, Java implementation (Filterer<G, E>, Predicate<? super E>), and relationship to related patterns.

https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/util/function/Predicate.html — Java's built-in Predicate<T> functional interface, providing and(), or(), negate(), and static isEqual(Object); the foundation of every Java filterer implementation.

Martin Fowler, Collection Pipeline (2015) — https://martinfowler.com/articles/collection-pipeline/ — introduces the programming pattern of chaining collection operations (filter, map, reduce) as a sequence that composes by passing collections between stages; filterer is a form of pipeline source that encapsulates its own traversal.

Eric Evans & Martin Fowler, Specification Pattern (2003) — https://martinfowler.com/apsupp/spec.pdf — the canonical paper; Evans' DDD Specification: an object wrapping a business rule (isSatisfiedBy) that can be composed (and/or/not) and used for in-memory selection, validation, and database query translation. Filterer differs by binding the criterion to a specific container and returning a filtered copy of that container's own type.

Ardalis.Specification — https://github.com/ardalis/specification — the most widely used .NET Specification pattern library (NuGet: Ardalis.Specification), providing base Specification<T>, base ISpecification<T>, and reusable specification implementations for the repository pattern.
https://www.javacodegeeks.com/2019/02/filterer-pattern-10-steps.html — Java Code Geeks reprint of the 10-step tutorial, extending the pattern's reach in the Java community.

Software Patterns Lexicon, Specification Pattern (2026) — https://softwarepatternslexicon.com/java/behavioral-patterns/specification-pattern/ — detailed comparison of Specification vs Predicate, when to use each, factory-method vs lambda tradeoffs, and translation to JPA Criteria.

Software Patterns Lexicon, Java Function Composition (2024) — https://softwarepatternslexicon.com/java/functional-programming-patterns-in-java/composing-functions-and-pipelines/ — comprehensive guide to composing Function, Predicate, Consumer, and stream pipelines in Java; covers tap/peek, error handling in composed pipelines, and testing strategy.

Guava Predicates — https://guava.dev/releases/23.4-jre/api/docs/com/google/common/base/Predicates.html — provides static factory predicates (and, or, not, compose, etc.) extending Java's Predicate interface with function composition via Predicates.compose(Predicate, Function).

Java Design Patterns, Function Composition — https://java-design-patterns.com/patterns/function-composition/ — describes composing small functions into single reusable operations; relates to filterer in that criteria composition (and/or/not) is itself a form of function composition.

OneUptime, API Filtering Patterns (2026) — https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-01-30-api-filtering-patterns/ — compares Specification, Criteria, Filter Chain, and Query Builder patterns for API-level filtering, including when to combine them.

dobtco/filterer — https://github.com/dobtco/filterer — Ruby gem (MIT) that adopted the pattern's name for object-oriented ActiveRecord query building: a PersonFilterer class maps request parameters to where-clauses so a controller calls Person.filter(params); the filterer idea landing in the Rails filter-object space, with a built query as result rather than a same-typed container copy (project now unmaintained).

enisn/AutoFilterer — https://github.com/enisn/AutoFilterer — .NET (MIT, NuGet) mini filtering framework: ApplyFilter compiles a filter DTO into a LINQ expression tree over the queryable, keeping criteria inspectable data (OpenAPI 3.0-compatible) rather than opaque lambdas — the 'inspectable criteria' best practice realised in a shipped library.

redru/filters — https://github.com/redru/filters — Java (Apache-2.0) library making Filter<T> a composable first-class criterion value (filtering().thenFiltering(), objectEquals) applied via stream().filter(filter); criteria-as-values without a container wrapper.

JustSteveKing, The Second Pattern: Specification — https://www.juststeveking.com/articles/the-second-pattern-specification/ — criticism of criterion-as-object abstraction: a specification/query object is over-engineering for a small fixed set of filters, and a hand-kept in-memory predicate drifts from its query translation; run the same fixtures through both to catch divergence.

thoughtbot, A Case for Query Objects in Rails — https://thoughtbot.com/blog/a-case-for-query-objects-in-rails — when filter/query objects earn their keep (optional, reused, multi-table criteria) and an explicit caution against minting one per filter; the cost side of promoting criteria to first-class objects.

Oracle, Core J2EE Patterns - Intercepting Filter — https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/intercepting-filter.html — the request-chain 'filter' pattern that shares the word but not the intent (cross-cutting interception around a target, not element selection returning a same-typed copy); the disambiguation reference for Filterer's name.
